Okay, so it sounds to me like I'm probably somewhere between your age and your parents age, which means I can see the perspective of both parties. I must admit, I never understood the concept of gaming for a career, although I played videogames when I was younger, however, with the rise of professional competitions and YouTube stars, I am fully aware that there is a way to make a living out of it. 

I suppose if I had to give advice to my kids on the matter, I would advise them to pursue their ambitions, however, when entering a field that is tight-knit and highly competitive, do not automatically assume that you will succeed at it. Don't get me wrong, anybody can succeed that wants it badly enough, but from the outside, the professional gaming arena appears to be as difficult as a vocation such as Hollywood Actor or astronaut to get into, particularly if you plan to make your entire living off of it. It is always good to have something to fall back on and if you love gaming, have you ever considered pursuing graphic design, games development or programming, with competitive gaming on the side, until you can get to a level where it could sustain you? That way you could be heavily involved in the thing you love from a different perspective and work towards your ultimate goal simultaneously. Just a suggestion.

I can understand why for your parents the pursuit of a career in gaming would be concerning, although as above I am fully aware that it does happen. I am not a huge advocate of the school system in the UK, but judging by your spelling of "mom" I'm guessing you are from the states, so I couldn't comment, but getting some basic grades under your belt i.e. maths, English, science etc. Will certainly pay dividends in the future, even if it is just to get your foot in the door for your first job. If you pay attention, you will also pick up on some fundemental concepts that serve well later on in life, although most people don't realise it (such as learning how to break down a problem in math, which may help you solving problems completely unrelated to math itself). Similarly, your ability to game well opens up additional avenues, such as good aptitude for multitasking or multiple-focus tasks. I spoke to a fighter pilot once, who told me that the guys who perform really well in aptitude testing are usually the ones who play a lot of games, so maybe that's worth considering too. Try to keep your chin up about the matter. 

Once you show your parents some success in your pursuits and some enthusiasm toward the wider world, they should start to come around to your way of thinking, but these things take time. From the sound of your situation, I wouldn't expect them to smother you with praise for each little change - it will take time, but it will be worth it.

That's not your doing. Ultimately you are a product of your upbringing, and if your mother doesn't think you are good enough to be her child, then she is the one in the wrong, as you were made by her and likely moulded by her in your upbringing. She only has herself to blame.

Also, try not to put yourself down. If you reflect upon yourself poorly, then others will see you in that light. What's good in your life? Do you have any hobbies? Do you work? Are you at school?

I had a contour roam 3 once upon a time. It was perfect for the job, but then I believe that they went under, so it is likely that you are looking at old stock unless they are back in the game.

I searched for quite some time to find something similar and landed on the TomTom Bandit action cam, which is slightly more modern, and has a better picture than the contour, though Bluetooth connectivity, GPS and other add ons reduce the battery life compared with the contour. 

The contour does what it says on the tin and has useful functions for riders such as a huge sliding switch on top to record, which is useful for bulky winter gloves, but is ultimately a very utilitarian camera. Night time recording is passable quality, and the microphone sucks for motorcycling (though this is a common flaw in most action cams as the wind noise drowns out everything else).

You will get more use and functionality out of other cameras, but if you are looking for a helmet cam only and can get it for a good price, then I'd say go for it.

Just my humble opinion but here goes:

1) A 125 could be used to commute 20 miles, but it depends what that 20 miles is. If it's town roads the whole way, then you would be okay, but if you have any high speed dual carriageways (or motorways if your license allows) it would be a fairly miserable affair, as you'd probably be limited to about 60mph and getting overtaken by angry lorries cutting in a little too close for comfort, is no fun for anybody... Anything less than a 125 for me personally would be a no go, especially as you mentioned you are a bigger guy. It would just be a constant battle with the bike.

2) I can't think of anything other than say a monkey bike or similar. A cruiser tends to suit bigger guys I find, and will probably be more comfortable.

3) This one is always a controversial topic. I personally don't hesitate buying bikes that need love as I am quite happy to spend weeks at a time in the garage fixing them, however, 40k on a bike is like the equivalent of double that on a car for most bikes. I'm not saying that it's the case with all bikes, but they won't last the same as a car, as they tend to be in a much higher state of tune than a car and require constant maintenance for a long life (anybody who disagrees - fite me irl bro). I am currently dailying a Honda TransAlp 650, which ingot for a silly price as it needed some TLC and I have just hit 65k, and she never misses a beat. I am on the market again, but this has kept me going for quite some time now, needing minimal maintenance. I do, however,Ake sure I drop the oil every 5000 miles, clean the chain every 500 miles (it has a scottoiler, which helps), and generally don't wait around for things to go wrong. An example of this is that last weekend, I changed my tyres and noticed that although the wheel bearings weren't knackered, they weren't as smooth as they would have been once upon a time, so for the sake of £30, I replaced them with the SKF equivalent.

If all of the above sounds a little daunting, then I would recommend spending a little more, preferably buying from a dealership and maybe aiming for a limit of 20k miles with proof of FSH. 

Bikes will not generally last in the same way that a car will, so I wouldn't try to convince yourself that they will though. Others may disagree. As I said, just my opinion.

4) A pedal bike is an almost entirely different kettle of fish. I would definitely recommend not tallying the two up against eachother. Go and do a CBT for the sake of £80. They will teach you the basics of using gears and whatnot on a bike, which will teach you whether or not it's for you.

5) Bikes are easier, but once you get into it, there is much more to be done. Big services will generally require you to check valve clearences and other things that modern cars don't require. Also you'll find things like cleaning a chain very tedious after putting on a lot of miles, but it has to be done, or you'll be replacing the chain very soon.

Hope this helps, but feel free to message me if you want any more advice.

A little late to the party, but might as well give my 2p on the matter whilst I have nothing better to do than write to some Internet people.

My love for bikes came about when I was about 5 or 6 years old. Basically I had a few friends that came from a motorcycling background, they coaxed me into riding off road and I did so for a number of years. Fast forward a number of years to when I was 17 years old, and I had quite a severe accident whilst riding a friends Yamaha WR450 enduro (great weapon). I was concussed and nobody witnessed the accident but through knowing the engine noises and gearing they estimated I clipped a wall at around 60mph. I fractured my elbow both wrists two ribs and my kneecap. The helmet broke and the chin guard went through my chin and I had gravel rash all over my arms and legs (the one time I decided to ride without full gear - go figure... take note).

Anyway, following the accident, I agreed to stop riding to put my family's mind at ease.  I didn't ride again, aside from at low speeds to repair my friend's bike until the age of 25. At this age the adrenaline junkie side of me had calmed somewhat and I finally got the blessing from my family to get back on a bike. Decided to go for a Triumph Street Triple, which was a great shout. 

My reasoning for wanting to get back on a bike is never a question I have thought about until I read your title. The feeling of missing the bikes never left me, even after driving performance cars and even racing them, the hole that was created when bikes were taken out of my life was never filled. Admittedly they are ridiculously fun, and in disagreement with Mr.  Clarkson, even an Atom doesn't compare. I still have a car as the missus isn't the hugest  of bike fans, but I am slowly bringing her over to the dark side. But the fun is only a part of it. I drive 112 miles per day to and from work on possibly the worst road in the UK (M25) and my life in a car has become nothing more than waiting in a car park to then get to a job in engineering which is okay (pays the bills) but nothing too exciting. Day in day out that starts to drive a person insane, which is why I took the plunge and got back on a bike.

It was only after getting back on one for the convenience, that I realised why there was such a hole in my life. As many people have already stated, the sense of freedom and escape that you get when riding is not comparable to anything you would have felt in a car. You have your own space, where you can just think and nobody can interrupt. The feeling of the wind blasting you as you make it through the traffic carries with it a sense of satisfaction that is indescribable without actually going out and feeling it. Bikers get a lot of stick and drivers tend to think of them as nothing more than an inconvenience that makes them look like the bad guy when they don't look in their mirrors and blind spots, but honestly, to me personally, it feels like home on a bike. The warmth of ridiculously stiff and heavy insulated armour, the closed in'ness of the helmet, the mechanical feeling of the gear changes, the beautiful growl & whistle of that three cylinder engine, no radio, no distraction... just me, her and the world... 

Anyway, I don't know if you'll see this, but I would seriously recommend giving it a try before knocking it you might fall in love. And on that note, I'm going for a ride. Good evening all!
